h: Two days in June 1314, and where to feel them
p: The battle wasn't one quick clash. It played out over two days, 23 and 24 June 1314. On the first day comes the tale everyone remembers: the English knight Sir Henry de Bohun spotted Robert the Bruce out in front of his troops and charged at him. Bruce, on a smaller horse, dodged the lance and brought his axe down on de Bohun's helmet. Legend has it his only complaint afterwards was that he'd broken his good axe.

On the second day the Scots pushed forward on boggy, cramped ground near the Bannock Burn, and Edward II's army was routed. Edward escaped, but the defeat was a huge blow, and Bannockburn became a rallying point in Scotland's story ever since.

The memorial itself is worth knowing about. The great bronze of Bruce on horseback is by Charles Pilkington Jackson and was unveiled in 1964 for the 650th anniversary, alongside the circular rotunda. Nearby is the Borestone, traditionally said to be where Bruce set up his command post.

Want to keep the history theme going? Cambuskenneth Abbey, on the edge of Stirling, is where Bruce held a parliament in 1326, and its tall bell tower still stands. The Kelpies and the Falkirk Wheel are both an easy drive away too, a brilliant change of pace if the kids have had their fill of battles.
